title: Bayesian Unsupervised Topic Segmentation
research_question: Can a Bayesian lexical-cohesion model support unsupervised linear topic segmentation and incorporate cue words to improve segmentation of meeting transcripts and textbook chapters?
methodology: Model a sentence as a bag of words from its segment multinomial, constrain segment indices to a linear sequence, and optimize a uniform-valid-segmentation prior with either posterior-mean language models or marginalized Dirichlet compound multinomials (S01–S05). The cohesion-only BAYESSEG uses dynamic programming. Cue variants emit the first word of each segment-initial sentence from a corpus-shared cue multinomial, requiring Metropolis-Hastings inference; BAYESSEG-CUE-PROP biases proposals toward a prior linguistic cue list (S06–S07). Priors are re-estimated from unlabeled corpus text. Compare three Bayesian variants with U&I, MCS, and LCSEG on ICSI transcripts and author-sectioned medical textbook chapters, with provided segment counts and Pk/WD evaluation (S08–S13). Printed equation issues are retained in T06-I05–I06.

analytic_results.posterior_mean: θ̂_{j,i}=(n_{j,i}+θ_0)/(N_j+Wθ_0); θ_0=1 recovers the stated U&I likelihood model; θ_0=0 gives the segment-word-count-weighted negative-entropy objective.

key_findings.finding: The target is a linear partition at sentence boundaries. Each sentence has one segment index, and the index can stay fixed or increase to the next segment; it cannot return to an earlier segment. This is not a representation of overlapping or recurring work-matter identity.
key_findings.quote: We will assume that topic breaks occur at sen- tence boundaries, and write zt to indicate the topic assignment for sentence t.
key_findings.evidence_basis: explicit_model_definition; capability implication is analyst interpretation

key_findings.finding: All experiments receive the desired segment count. Cohesion-only inference uses dynamic programming; cue-based inference pools boundary-word counts across documents and uses Metropolis-Hastings moves that preserve segment count.
key_findings.quote: In all exper- iments, we assume that the number of desired seg- ments is provided.

key_findings.finding: On the medical-textbook chapter-to-section task with provided segment counts, BAYESSEG and BAYESSEG-CUE tie at Pk 0.339 and WD 0.353. The best respective non-Bayesian baselines are MCS Pk 0.368 and U&I WD 0.376. These are observed error reductions of 0.029 and 0.023; significance of system differences is not reported.

On ICSI meeting segmentation with provided segment counts, Table 1 gives BAYESSEG Pk/WD 0.264/0.319, BAYESSEG-CUE 0.261/0.316, and BAYESSEG-CUE-PROP 0.258/0.312. Cues reduce both reported meeting errors. On textbooks, ordinary cues tie cohesion-only results; the linguistic proposal raises both errors to 0.343/0.355.

The Section 6 suggestion that loss of exact inference may explain a decline for meetings conflicts with Table 1 and the preceding statement that cues improve meetings. The intended dataset name cannot be established from this paper.
key_findings.quote: the addition of cue phrases prevents the use of exact inference techniques, which may ex- plain the decline in results for the meetings dataset.

key_findings.finding: For meeting cue discovery, the paper reports four of its top ten cue words also identified by Galley et al.’s supervised procedure. The PDF visibly marks okay, so, and, and but with asterisks, confirming four rather than the three suspected in the parent pre-read. This is cue-list overlap, not gold or predicted Topic-span overlap.
key_findings.quote: Four of the ten cue phrases identified by our system overlap with their analysis; these are indicated with asterisks.

key_findings.finding: The textbook corpus is divided into ten parts for separate inference because of memory constraints. This is unsupervised corpus pooling within memory partitions, not supervised ten-fold evaluation. Partition membership, sizes, duplicate controls, and held-out testing are not reported.
key_findings.quote: Due to mem- ory constraints, we divide the textbook dataset into ten parts, and perform inference in each part sepa- rately.

key_findings.finding: The prose states that Bayesian systems perform 4–5% better than the best baseline on meeting Pk. Table 1’s best non-Bayesian Pk is U&I 0.297, giving reductions of 3.3, 3.6, and 3.9 percentage points, or 11.11%, 12.12%, and 13.13% relative, across the three Bayesian variants. The prose range does not match these displayed values under either convention.
key_findings.quote: On the ICSI meeting corpus, the Bayesian systems perform 4-5% better than the best baseline on the Pk metric, and achieve smaller improvement on the WindowDiff metric.

key_findings.finding: The authors suggest that pooling cue counts over the entire textbook corpus might improve results compared with the ten-part configuration. The paper reports no full-corpus comparison, so this remains an untested explanation rather than a measured gain.
key_findings.quote: We may achieve better results by performing inference over the entire dataset simultaneously, due to pooling counts for cue phrases across all docu- ments.

limitations: Sentence-only, exclusive, contiguous segment membership cannot directly express one span assigned to multiple Topics or a Topic recurring across separated spans (T06-F01; S01).
Every experiment assumes provided segment count; no unknown-count evaluation is reported (T06-F02; S11).
No email or asynchronous work-message experiment is reported. The two domains are meeting transcripts and textbook chapters (S08).
No evaluation measures retained conditions, evidence, exceptions, action scope, approval scope, or reply scope. This is absent evaluation, not a measured failure (S09, S13, S17).
IAA, annotator population/instructions, exact meeting scoring IDs, window size, scored-window counts, document aggregation, and duplicate controls are not reported (S08–S11).
The ten textbook parts are memory partitions. No held-out test or inductive transfer claim is established by this corpus-level unsupervised setting (T06-F07).
Sampling results average five runs without variance or significance tests of segmentation differences. Table 2 chi-squared significance concerns cue occurrences, not system superiority (S10, S17).
The loss-of-exact-inference explanation, reported gain ranges, and printed likelihood/proposal issues require the qualifications in T06-I01–I06.
The approximately three-minute runtime lacks hardware and detailed dataset/variant timing; it provides no Raspberry Pi, incremental, or production latency evidence (S10).

material_inconsistencies.conflicting_evidence: Across every Table 1 textbook Bayesian/non-Bayesian pair and metric, absolute improvements range from 0.021 to 0.032 (2.1–3.2 percentage points). This roughly matches rounded prose but is not an exact interval; relative reductions range from 5.5851% to 8.3784%.

material_inconsistencies.source_statement: Prose: four of the top ten meeting cues overlap the supervised list. Parent pre-read suspected only three displayed stars.
material_inconsistencies.verified_evidence: Original Table 2 has four: okay*, so*, and*, but*. Raw, rough, layout, and page-indexed conversions also retain all four. There is no surviving paper count inconsistency.

material_inconsistencies.source_statement: Section 3.2 prints Γ(n_{j,i}+Wθ_0)/Γ(θ_0) inside the DCM product, while equation (2) treats θ_0 as a per-word prior.
material_inconsistencies.analyst_interpretation: The per-word prior implies Γ(n_{j,i}+θ_0)/Γ(θ_0), derived analytically. Also, equation (7) first multiplies sentence marginals although the model shares a multinomial within each segment. The PDF confirms the source formulas; implementation behavior is unknown.

material_inconsistencies.source_statement: Section 4.2 says exponential decay but prints d^λ; its linguistic proposal prints q_ling(z′|z′) although the right side is q(z′|z).
material_inconsistencies.analyst_interpretation: The displayed distance weighting is a power law. The proposal-conditioning notation also conflicts with the description of a move from z to z′. Do not silently repair either when reproducing the method.

RQ1.answer: Sentence granularity is an assumption, not a comparison of scope-preserving units.

RQ2.answer: No email/asynchronous clustering or interleaving representation.

RQ3.answer: Documents can contain multiple sequential segments; gold semantic multi-membership is not annotated, and the model predicts one segment per sentence.

RQ4.strength: negative capability inference, not negative experiment
RQ4.answer: Monotone segment indices exclude recurring segment identity and overlap; Table 2 list overlap is unrelated.

RQ5.answer: No direct work-text preservation evaluation. Potential scope loss needs separate tests.

RQ6.answer: Keep Pk and WD separate; report known K, missing window denominators, relative versus absolute gains, and retained source inconsistencies.

RQ7.answer: Corpus counts and memory partitions are reported; IAA, exact IDs, duplicate controls, and several scoring details are missing.

RQ8.answer: Use as a controlled contiguous-sentence baseline and test separate representation/preservation extensions. No architecture is approved.

interpretation.text: The method is a candidate baseline for boundary placement where a contiguous partition is appropriate. Lexical distributions and document membership do not establish the user’s concrete work-matter identity.
Sharing a cue multinomial across documents shares a discourse feature, not semantic Topic identity. Drawing a cue token from a different language model does not implement span multi-membership.

A sentence containing an action plus a condition or evidence relevant to another Topic could require finer or overlapping assignments. The partition may force a choice, but this paper does not measure scope loss or establish a preferred replacement unit.

Corpus-dependent cue gains justify testing cue features on reviewed email examples; the meeting gain cannot be assumed to transfer. Textbook results already show that adding the feature is not uniformly beneficial.

proposed_experiments.design: Compare a sentence-partition baseline with clause, EDU, arbitrary-span, and hybrid annotation on the same reviewed work messages. Allow multiple Topics per span and non-contiguous spans per Topic in gold.
proposed_experiments.evaluation: Measure representable gold evidence and exact/overlap span scores separately from boundary Pk/WD; retain source offsets and uncertainty.

proposed_experiments.design: Evaluate the contiguous baseline under provided segment counts and separately estimated counts. Compare cohesion-only and cue variants with fixed preprocessing and repeated seeds.
proposed_experiments.evaluation: Report Pk and WD with explicit window, corpus aggregation, per-message counts, and variance. Keep thread/source/time holdouts separate from unsupervised inference partitions; audit quoted duplicates.

proposed_experiments.design: Use public or synthetic examples with conditions, exceptions, evidence, approvals, actions, and selective replies. Mark which text must remain linked to each concrete work matter.
proposed_experiments.evaluation: Measure omitted and broadened decision-bearing scope separately, including shared spans and recurring evidence. Report these results separately from segmentation penalties.

proposed_experiments.design: Before implementation comparison, resolve the printed DCM/proposal equations against any authorized frozen code and document the implemented formulas; test corpus-wide versus partitioned cue fitting if resources permit.
proposed_experiments.evaluation: Use controlled segmentation scores and measured memory/runtime; keep the author’s full-pooling hypothesis unconfirmed until tested.
